nameStory: The great spider crab gets its name from its long, spindly legs that sprawl outward like a spider's, making it look more arachnid than crustacean. The 'great' part refers to the impressive size these crabs can reach after multiple molts throughout their lives. When you see one scuttling across the ocean floor, that spider-like silhouette is unmistakable.
description: The great spider crab is a fascinating deep-water crustacean with extremely long, thin legs that give it an almost alien appearance. Unlike the broad, flat crabs you might find under beach rocks, this species has a more triangular body and legs that can span considerably when extended. These crabs live primarily below the tide line in the cold waters of the North Atlantic, including New England's deeper coastal areas. They're part of the same group as lobsters and other crabs (called decapods, meaning 'ten feet').

idTips.label: Spider-like leg arrangement
idTips.description: Eight extremely long, thin legs that extend outward from a relatively small body, creating an unmistakable spider-like silhouette when viewed from above or below

idTips.label: Triangular body shape
idTips.description: Body (called the carapace) is roughly triangular rather than round or oval, with a pointed front end that narrows to a distinct rostrum or beak

idTips.label: Rough, bumpy shell texture
idTips.description: The outer shell feels coarse and bumpy to the touch, often with small spines or tubercles that create an irregular surface unlike smooth-shelled crabs

idTips.label: Mottled coloration
idTips.description: Usually displays browns, grays, and sometimes reddish tones in a mottled pattern that helps camouflage against rocky seafloor

idTips.label: Claws relatively small
idTips.description: Front claws are noticeably smaller and more delicate compared to the crab's overall leg span, unlike lobsters or large shore crabs

habitat: Great spider crabs live in deeper New England waters, typically below the low tide line in rocky or sandy bottom areas. You're most likely to encounter them if you're diving, fishing in deeper water, or find one occasionally washed up after storms. They prefer the cooler waters of the Gulf of Maine and areas with good water circulation.

seasonality.spring: Active in deeper waters as temperatures begin to warm. This is molting season for many individuals, when they shed their old shells to grow larger.
seasonality.summer: Most active period, with crabs moving more freely in the warmer water. Occasionally found in slightly shallower areas during this time.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper, more stable temperature zones. Any storm-washed specimens are most likely found during fall storms.
seasonality.winter: Less active in the coldest waters, staying in deeper areas. Rarely encountered except by deep-water fishermen or divers.

funFact: These crabs are living escape artists that can literally walk out of their own skin! When they molt, they back completely out of their old shell through a crack in the back, leaving behind a perfect empty crab shell that looks like a ghost version of themselves - and they can do this multiple times throughout their lives to keep growing.
confusionNotes: The main confusion is with the contracted crab, its close relative, but great spider crabs are generally larger with longer legs and a more pronounced triangular body shape. Think 'great' equals greater size and longer leg span - if it looks impressively spidery, it's likely the great spider crab.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'spider crab,' these are true crabs, not spiders - they're actually more closely related to lobsters than to any arachnid. The spider comparison is purely about their leg arrangement and movement style.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the contracted crab, the great spider crab lives up to its name by being larger overall with noticeably longer legs and a more elongated body shape. The contracted crab appears more compact and 'pulled in' as its name suggests, while the great spider crab sprawls outward dramatically. Both have that characteristic triangular body, but the great spider crab's proportions are more exaggerated in every dimension.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its closest relative in New England waters, the great spider crab, the contracted crab has that distinctive pinched waist that makes its shell look like an hourglass or lyre.
